25: Lecture two. Looking at shape before looking at numbers. We will cover distributions, summary statistics and robust statistics: skewness, kurtosis, outliers, and the mean, median and I Q R.
26: Why does shape matter? Because a single number can hide the picture. Look at three distributions with the same statistic, the mean. In a symmetric distribution, the mean lands in the middle and describes almost everybody. In a two group distribution, the mean lands in the gap and describes nobody in the data. In a right skewed distribution, the mean already sits above most of the bars, pulled by the tail. Same statistic, three different realities. That is why we plot first and summarise second.
27: Every distribution answers three questions. First, where is it? That is the centre, measured by mean, median or mode. Second, how wide is it? That is the spread, measured by range, standard deviation or I Q R. Third, what shape is it? That is skewness, kurtosis, and any stray points. Skewness and kurtosis are simply numbers that describe question three.
28: Skewness tells you which way the tail points. Left skewed, or negative skew, has a long tail on the left, like exam marks where most students score high. Symmetric, with skew near zero, has both tails alike, like heights or measurement error. Right skewed, or positive skew, has a long tail on the right, like income, house prices or waiting times. Remember this: the tail names the skew, not the hump. A right skewed distribution has most of its data on the left.
29: Skew pulls the mean, not the median. Here is the ordering rule. In a right skewed distribution, mode is less than median, which is less than mean. In a symmetric one, all three are roughly equal. In a left skewed one, mean is less than median, which is less than mode. This is why average income is always higher than what a typical person earns. A few very large values sit in the tail, and only the mean feels them. So report the median whenever the tail is long.
30: Kurtosis tells you how often extreme values happen. It measures the weight in the tails, not the sharpness of the peak. High kurtosis means extreme values arrive more often than a bell curve would predict. We use excess kurtosis, which is kurtosis minus three, so a normal curve scores zero. Above zero means heavy tails and more outliers expected. Below zero means light tails, with values staying near the centre. In the picture, both curves have the same centre and spread, but the amber curve keeps more of its data far from the middle, so rare events are not so rare.
31: There are three families. Platykurtic, excess kurtosis below zero: thin tails, extreme values are genuinely rare, and averages behave well. Mesokurtic, excess kurtosis near zero: the bell curve benchmark, where standard textbook rules apply. Leptokurtic, excess kurtosis above zero: fat tails, where shocks and outliers are common and standard deviation understates the risk. Practically, high kurtosis is a warning that your outlier check is about to find something.
32: Now outliers, and the box plot that finds them. The I Q R is Q three minus Q one, the width of the middle fifty percent of the data. The fences are Q one minus one point five times I Q R, and Q three plus one point five times I Q R. Points outside the fences are flagged as outliers. An outlier is a point far from the bulk of the data, and far needs a definition. The one point five I Q R rule is the usual one because it is built from quartiles, so the outliers themselves cannot move it. Most importantly: a flag is a question, not a verdict.
33: Before you delete anything, remember there are three reasons a point sits far out. One, a mistake, like an age recorded as nine ninety nine, a sensor reading during a power cut, or a misplaced decimal. Fix it or remove it, and say so in the report. Two, rare but real, like a genuinely huge order or a patient with an unusual response. Keep it. This is often the most interesting row in the dataset. Three, the wrong population, like a wholesale buyer inside retail customer data. Separate it out and analyse the groups apart. Deleting every flagged point is the fastest way to produce a tidy, wrong analysis.
34: Here is the toolkit of summary statistics, sorted by what they tell you. For centre: the mean is the balance point and breaks down when one extreme value drags it. The median is the middle value and rarely breaks down. The mode is the most common value and fails when data is continuous or has ties. For spread: the range depends on just two points. Standard deviation is the typical distance from the mean, and skew or outliers inflate it. The I Q R is the width of the middle fifty percent and is very stable. For shape: skewness says which side the tail is on, but is noisy in small samples. Kurtosis says how heavy the tails are, and is very sensitive to a few points. Always report a centre and a spread together. One without the other is half a description.
35: Why does robustness matter? Take seven monthly salaries, in thousands: twenty eight, thirty, thirty two, thirty three, thirty five, thirty eight and forty two. Now the manager joins, earning four hundred. The mean more than doubles, from about thirty five to eighty, and now describes nobody in the room. The median moves by one unit, from thirty three to thirty four. Nothing changed for seven of the eight people. A statistic that one row can move this far is not a summary. It is a hostage.
36: So which do you report? If the histogram looks symmetric with no stray points, use mean and standard deviation. If the tail is long on one side, use median and I Q R, and say the data is skewed. If there are a handful of extreme points with unknown cause, report both and show how much they differ. If you compare groups of very different sizes, use median, I Q R, and a box plot per group. And in every case, put the picture next to the number. The histogram is the evidence, and the statistic is only the caption.
37: Remember this much. Plot first, summarise second. Skewness says which side the tail is on, and the tail names the skew, not the hump. Kurtosis says how heavy the tails are, meaning how often extremes should be expected. The one point five I Q R fence flags candidates, so investigate them and do not sweep them away. Use mean and standard deviation for tidy symmetric data, and median and I Q R for everything else.
38: Six mistakes that cost marks and credibility. One, deleting outliers silently: always state the rule, the count and the effect on the result. Two, reporting the mean of a skewed column: it is technically true but practically misleading, so give the median alongside it. Three, using absolute z greater than three on a small sample: the ceiling is n minus one over root n, so on eleven rows nothing can exceed three point zero two. Four, treating a sentinel as a number: zero millimetres of mercury, minus one, nine ninety nine, or the date nineteen hundred are missing values in disguise. Five, testing a hypothesis that the same data suggested: the p value you print is not the p value you mean. Six, trusting one plot: always use at least two views, like a box plot plus a histogram.
39: To take away from lectures one and two. One, exploration is a habit that runs through the whole lifecycle, not a stage you finish. Two, explore freely, confirm strictly, and never on the same rows. Three, a bigger sample shrinks noise, but only a better sample removes bias. Four, summary statistics compress, and compression loses structure, so plot it. Five, shape first, summary second: skewness tells you which centre to trust, and kurtosis tells you how surprised to be by the tails. Six, the median and I Q R survive contamination, while the mean, standard deviation and range do not.
